lead: A receiving antenna is a transmitting antenna used the other way round: the incoming wave induces a voltage, and the antenna drives the receiver like a source in series with its own impedance. Reciprocity makes the pattern, impedance and gain the same in both roles. Effective length turns a field strength into volts, and effective area turns a power density into watts.
prereq: You need: effective aperture and the polarization loss factor (radiation resistance, efficiency and aperture).

sections.h3: The receiving antenna as a Thevenin source

blocks.text: A wave of field strength E (V/m) arriving at an antenna pushes charge along the metal. At the open terminals this appears as a voltage
Voc = E leff cos ψ. Voc in V; leff is the effective length in m; ψ is the angle between the field and the antenna’s own polarization direction

Seen from the receiver, the antenna is a source V<sub>oc</sub> in series with its impedance Z<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub> + jX<sub>A</sub>, the same impedance it shows as a transmitter. A load Z<sub>L</sub> takes the current I = V<sub>oc</sub>/(Z<sub>A</sub> + Z<sub>L</sub>) and the power ½|I|² R<sub>load</sub>. The most power flows with a conjugate match, Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>A</sub>* (R<sub>load</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>, X<sub>load</sub> = −X<sub>A</sub>), and then
PL = |Voc|² / (8(Rr + RL)). the available power in W, with Voc a peak value

Under that match, for a lossless antenna, an equal power is re-radiated (scattered) through R<sub>r</sub>: half of what the antenna collects reaches the load. With loss, R<sub>L</sub> takes its share as heat. Any mismatch costs a further factor 1 − |Γ|².

Effective length is the length of a uniform current element that would give the same Voc. It depends on the current distribution: leff = l for the Hertzian dipole (uniform current), leff = l/2 for a centre-fed short dipole (triangular current), and leff = λ/π ≈ 0.318λ for a half-wave dipole, not its physical λ/2.
The link between effective area and directivity can be checked on the Hertzian dipole, using only results of this unit:

items: Matched, broadside: V<sub>oc</sub> = E l, so P<sub>L</sub> = E² l² / (8R<sub>r</sub>) = E² l² / (8 × 80π² l²/λ²) = E² λ² / (640π²).
Power density of the wave: S = E²/(2η) = E²/(240π).

blocks.text: Since D = 1.5 for this dipole, Aem = D λ²/4π. Reciprocity makes this ratio Aem/D = λ²/4π the same for every antenna, so it holds in general. The capture area of a thin wire is far larger than its metal: a short dipole at 100 MHz has Aem = 1.5 × 9/4π = 1.07 m². With polarization mismatch the received power is Pr = S Ae × PLF.

Take two antennas, 1 and 2, in any linear medium. Drive antenna 1 with current I₁ and measure the open-circuit voltage V₂ at antenna 2; then drive antenna 2 with the same current and measure V₁ at antenna 1. The reciprocity theorem says the two transfer impedances are equal: Z₂₁ = V₂/I₁ = V₁/I₂ = Z₁₂, even if the antennas are quite different. A network with this property is reciprocal, like any circuit of resistors, inductors and capacitors.

items: Pattern: moving antenna 2 round antenna 1 maps the same pattern whether 1 transmits or receives.
Impedance: the self-impedance Z₁₁ seen at the terminals is the same in both roles, so a match found on transmit holds on receive.
Gain and effective area: they are tied by A<sub>e</sub> = Gλ²/4π, so a gain measured on transmit gives the receiving area.

blocks.text: Received powers are not automatically equal in the two directions. They are equal when the two set-ups are identical (same source and load impedances, same current), which is how an antenna range uses one measurement for both roles. Reciprocity fails with ferrites in a magnetic field or with the ionosphere in the Earth’s field, which are non-reciprocal media; circulators and isolators use this on purpose.

examples.question: A short dipole (D = 1.5) receives a 100 MHz wave of power density S = 10 µW/m², polarization matched. Find its maximum effective aperture and the power delivered to a conjugate-matched load, in watts and dBm.

A resonant half-wave dipole (Z<sub>A</sub> = 73 Ω, D = 1.64) receives a 100 MHz wave of field strength 1 mV/m (peak), polarization matched. Find (a) V<sub>oc</sub>, (b) the power into a matched 73 Ω load, (c) the same power from S and A<sub>em</sub>, and (d) the power into a 50 Ω receiver.
steps: (b) P<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>oc</sub>²/(8R<sub>r</sub>) = (0.955 × 10⁻³)²/(8 × 73) = 1.56 × 10⁻⁹ W = 1.56 nW, that is −58.1 dBm.
(c) S = E²/(2η) = 10⁻⁶/754 = 1.326 × 10⁻⁹ W/m²; A<sub>em</sub> = 1.64 × 9/4π = 1.175 m² (1.177 with D = 1.641); P = S A<sub>em</sub> = 1.56 × 10⁻⁹ W. The two routes agree.
examples.answer: V<sub>oc</sub> = 0.955 mV; 1.56 nW (−58.1 dBm) matched, by both routes; 1.51 nW into 50 Ω, a 0.15 dB mismatch loss.

traps: Using l<sub>eff</sub> = l for a real short dipole. With triangular current it is l/2; l is only for uniform current.
Using the physical λ/2 for a half-wave dipole. Its effective length is λ/π.
Writing the match as Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>A</sub>. Maximum power needs the conjugate, Z<sub>L</sub> = Z<sub>A</sub>*.
Thinking the matched load gets all the captured power. For a lossless antenna half is re-radiated through R<sub>r</sub>.
Saying reciprocity makes the received powers equal in both directions for any two antennas. It makes the transfer impedances equal; equal powers need identical source and load set-ups.

quiz.q: State the Thevenin model of a receiving antenna.
quiz.a: A source V<sub>oc</sub> = E l<sub>eff</sub> cos ψ in series with Z<sub>A</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub> + jX<sub>A</sub>, the antenna’s transmitting impedance.

quiz.q: State the reciprocity theorem for two antennas.
quiz.a: The transfer impedances are equal: the open-circuit voltage at antenna 2 per unit current in antenna 1 equals the voltage at 1 per unit current in 2, Z₂₁ = Z₁₂.

quiz.q: Why is a conjugate match used at the receiver terminals?
quiz.a: It cancels X<sub>A</sub> and makes R<sub>load</sub> = R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>, which by the maximum power transfer theorem draws the available power |V<sub>oc</sub>|²/(8(R<sub>r</sub> + R<sub>L</sub>)) from the source.

quiz.q: A half-wave dipole receives at 300 MHz. Find l<sub>eff</sub>, and V<sub>oc</sub> for a matched field of 2 mV/m.
A polarization-matched antenna with D = 2 at 1 GHz sees S = 1 mW/m². Find P<sub>r</sub>.
Why can A<sub>e</sub> exceed the physical area of a wire antenna?
quiz.a: A<sub>e</sub> = Dλ²/4π depends on directivity and wavelength, not on the metal. The induced current re-radiates a field that bends the incoming power flow towards the wire, so it collects power from an area of order λ².

quiz.q: Reciprocity says the patterns are identical. Why does it not follow that the power received in each direction of a link is equal?
quiz.a: Reciprocity equates the transfer impedances Z₁₂ and Z₂₁. The actual powers also depend on the source, the drive current and each load. Only with identical set-ups at both ends are the received powers equal.

beyond: Not for the exam. Time-division 5G and Wi-Fi reuse the uplink channel estimate for downlink beamforming, relying on reciprocity of the air path; RFID tags switch their load to change the power they scatter back. A receiving antenna also picks up noise, its antenna temperature (see noise figure, cascaded noise and sensitivity). Search next for “antenna temperature” and “backscatter RFID”.
